headline: Fat Bear Week opens. Can Chunk win again?
summary: Fat Bear Week is open in Alaska. The public votes, and the crown goes to the fattest bear. Last year it went to Chunk, 1,200 pounds of bear, and Chunk is back to defend it. The AP's question is whether a champion that size can win twice. The Hill's advice is simpler: get your ballot ready.

cover_question.q: Is it mean to call a bear fat?

cover_answer: No. Fat is what a bear wants before winter.
table_question: Should a contest be decided by a vote or by a scale?

5-7.script: In Alaska, people are voting for the fattest bear. Last year's winner is called Chunk and weighs 1,200 pounds, about as much as your whole class put together. Bears eat all summer so they can sleep through the winter, and a fat bear is a bear that did its job. Chunk is back this year to try to win again.
5-7.why: The whole class put together is a weight a six-year-old can feel. One vivid picture stands in for the story, and this one is a happy bear. At this age a child takes one detail for the whole event, so the detail is the winner, not the voting.
5-7.why_long: A five-year-old reasons from what is in front of them and takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script hands them the feature: a bear as heavy as the whole class, and fat is the bear's job. The vote can wait. Expect "can I vote?" Yes, with you, and the most picks wins.

8-12.script: Fat Bear Week is open in Alaska: people look at the bears and vote for the fattest. Bears eat all summer and sleep most of the winter, so the fat gets them through. Last year's champ, Chunk, is 1,200 pounds and back to defend. It runs like a class election: everyone looks, everyone votes.
8-12.why: A chain from summer eating to winter sleep, and a class election as the mechanism.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out cause and effect and how rules decide things, and the story hands them both: eat all summer, sleep all winter, so fat is the score, and a vote picks the winner, not a scale. The class election is the mechanism. Expect "is a vote fair if nobody weighs them?" Ask what a scale would change.

13-17.script: Is it mean to call a bear fat? Fat Bear Week opened in Alaska, and last year's champion, Chunk, is 1,200 pounds and back for more. For a bear, fat before winter is the job, and the vote is a compliment. Second: why do people who skip real elections turn out for a bear?
13-17.why: Two true things: fat is an insult for people and a prize for a bear.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: fat is a slur for a person and a trophy for a bear, and one word does both jobs. The second question is the real one, why a bear vote feels better than a ballot, and it only works if you answer honestly. Expect "do you vote?" Say the true thing, then ask why the bear is easier.

5-7.q: Is it okay for Chunk to be that fat?
5-7.a: Yes. Bears are meant to get fat before winter. It keeps them warm and fed while they sleep.

8-12.q: How do they know which bear is fattest?
8-12.a: People vote. The Hill says get your ballot ready.

8-12.q: Why do bears get fat on purpose?
8-12.a: They sleep most of the winter without eating. The fat is packed food.

13-17.q: Is it mean to call a bear fat?
13-17.a: No. Fat is what a bear wants before winter. The contest is a compliment.

13-17.q: Why do people vote for a bear?
13-17.a: It's fun, it's free, and nobody disputes the result. Why doesn't an election feel like that?
